q: my 2 year old has a fever of 102.5, should I give Tylenol?
text:
102.5 °F = 39.2 °C.

Yes, you can give acetaminophen (Tylenol) — it helps reduce fever in children, according to MedlinePlus [3]. The main goal is your child's comfort, not bringing the temperature itself down, and paracetamol and ibuprofen work similarly [1]. Give it at the dose your paediatrician recommends, every 4 to 6 hours, and know your child's weight before dosing [1][3]. Do not give aspirin to a child [3]. Keep them well hydrated and don't force food [1]. Get medical advice if you're worried or if the medicine isn't helping [4].

q: my baby is 7 months and has been warm since last night, 101.8 F
text:
A fever is a sign the body is fighting an infection, and most fevers in babies are caused by infections, according to MedlinePlus [1]. A temperature of 101.8 °F is a fever, and fever itself is not an illness [1]. Keep offering plenty of fluids, because it is important to drink enough to prevent dehydration [1]. If the fever is high, your health professional may recommend an over-the-counter medicine such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen [1]. Never give a child with fever aspirin [1].

See a doctor promptly if your baby is unusually irritable or low on energy, is not wetting nappies for 3 hours or more, is crying without tears, or has a dry mouth [6].

q: how many ml of Tylenol for a 22 pound baby
text:
A 22-pound baby weighs about 10 kg. With infant liquid that has 120 mg of acetaminophen in 5 ml, the NHS gives 5 ml for children 6 to 23 months old [3]. MedlinePlus says to know your child's weight before giving acetaminophen, and to give it every 4 to 6 hours [4].

- Do not give more than 4 doses in 24 hours [3].
- Always use the syringe or spoon that comes with the medicine to measure it [3].
- Do not give it for more than 3 days without speaking to a doctor or pharmacist [3].

q: my 3 year old keeps vomiting every time he drinks water
text:
Vomiting with gastroenteritis is usually not serious, but the main risk is dehydration from the fluid lost through vomiting and diarrhoea, according to the SEUP [2]. Offer an oral rehydration solution — it contains water, sugar and salts in the right proportion — in small amounts and frequent sips, after each vomit, so it is better tolerated [2]. Do not use homemade solutions or commercial soft drinks to replace those losses [6]. Keep offering food in smaller, more frequent amounts; avoid fatty foods, sweets and juices, and sports drinks [4].

See a doctor if he vomits a lot and cannot keep down solids or liquids, or vomits even when he takes nothing, or if the vomit is greenish, contains blood or looks like brown coffee grounds [4]. Also if he is very thirsty, cries without tears, urinates little or has sunken eyes [6].

q: how do I know if my child is getting dehydrated from vomiting
text: The main risk of vomiting is dehydration, according to the SEUP [1]. Dehydration happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in, and vomiting is one of the causes [3]. To prevent it, offer oral rehydration solution: if your child is listless, vomits many times or will not drink, see your doctor [1]. After a vomit, wait 20 minutes and then give oral rehydration solution, 2–5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour, and do not use homemade solutions or fizzy drinks [4]. Watch for vomiting a lot or not tolerating solids or liquids, and for vomit that is green, bloody or looks like coffee grounds — then seek care again [5].

q: my daughter has diarrhea since yesterday and doesnt want much food
text: Diarrhea in a child is usually gastroenteritis, an infection of the digestive tract that is not serious in healthy people but can sometimes lead to dehydration, according to MedlinePlus [2]. The most important thing at home is to prevent that dehydration by giving oral rehydration solution in small amounts and frequent sips, after each loose stool or vomit [4]. When she is taking liquids well, offer her food without forcing her, in small amounts, whatever she feels like — cereals, chicken, fruit and vegetables are usually well tolerated [5]. Avoid soft drinks and sugary juices, and skip chocolate, sweets, fried food and sauces [5]. See a doctor if she has diarrhea lasting more than a day, any fever, frequent loose stools or vomiting, signs of dehydration such as thirst, dry mouth, fewer wet diapers or no tears when crying, or if she refuses to eat or drink [1][3].

q: can I give Pedialyte after every loose stool
text:
Yes, children with diarrhoea should be given an oral rehydration solution to replace the fluids and electrolytes they lose, according to MedlinePlus [1]. The SEUP says the most important thing is to prevent dehydration using ready-made oral rehydration solutions, and that home-made solutions and commercial soft drinks should not be used to replace these losses [3]. The WHO also recommends oral rehydration salts, a mix of clean water, salt and sugar, which are absorbed in the small intestine and replace the water and electrolytes lost in the stools [4].

See a doctor if your child has signs of dehydration such as thirst, dry mouth, urinating less than usual or no wet nappies for 3 hours or more, or no tears when crying, according to MedlinePlus [2].

q: my 5 year old has been coughing all night, what can I do

A night cough in a preschooler is often linked to the same airways problem as wheezing, and viral colds are the main trigger at this age, according to the SEUP [1]. q: my baby has a cough and sounds very congested when sleeping
text:
A cough with a blocked, noisy nose is usually a common cold: sneezing, a stuffy nose, runny nose, sore throat and cough are the usual symptoms, and they can last 10 to 14 days, according to MedlinePlus [3].

q: my 3 year old has a barking cough but is breathing okay
text: A barking cough that sounds like a seal, with a hoarse voice and cold-like symptoms, is typical of croup, according to the NHS [3]. It is usually mild and gets better on its own within a few days, though it can last up to a week, and it is often worse at night [2][3]. Offer fluids and the usual fever medicine if there is a fever [2]. See a doctor if your child's breathing becomes difficult or noisy at rest, if the ribs or chest pull in, if they struggle to swallow or drool a lot, or if they seem worse or are not getting better [3][4].

See a doctor if your child is listless or very irritable, has trouble breathing, has spots that do not fade when you press them, or will not take fluids [1].

q: my baby has a diaper rash that isnt going away with cream
text: A rash that is not going away should be checked by your doctor, according to the NHS [6]. Most diaper rashes are not serious, but you should get it looked at if it does not go away, gets worse or spreads, if your baby has a high temperature, or if your baby seems very uncomfortable [6]. A doctor may prescribe a steroid cream for redness and soreness, an antifungal cream if they think it is a thrush infection, or antibiotics if they think it is a bacterial infection [2]. In the meantime, change wet or dirty diapers as soon as possible and apply a thin layer of barrier cream at each change [1][3]. Do not use soaps, baby lotion or bubble bath, talcum powder or antiseptic creams, and do not put diapers on too tightly [5].

q: my 6 year old fell from the bed and hit the back of his head
text:
Most head injuries in children are not serious, and most children recover quickly, according to the SEUP [1][6]. Common symptoms after a blow to the head are headache, confusion, brief memory loss, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness [1].

Watch him over the next 24 hours for warning signs, and get medical help if any appear [3][4]:

- Intense or worsening headache, or repeated vomiting [4]
- Confusion, difficulty speaking or walking, or unusual behaviour [4]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [4]
- He cannot be woken, or is very irritable or hard to rouse [4]

He can sleep, but after a more significant knock it is worth waking him every 4 hours [6]. If he has a headache, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose your doctor indicates [6].

q: when can I start giving my baby solid foods
text:
Around 6 months old is when babies are ready to start solid foods, according to the NHS [1]. At first, how much they eat matters less than getting used to the idea of eating — they still get most of their energy and nutrients from breast milk or infant formula [1].

Three signs together show your baby is ready: staying in a sitting position with a steady head, coordinating eyes, hands and mouth to pick up food and bring it to their mouth, and swallowing food rather than spitting it out [6]. Chewing fists, waking more at night, or wanting extra milk feeds are normal behaviours, not signs of readiness [6].

If your baby was born prematurely, ask your pediatrician for advice on when to start [1].

q: my 5 month old reaches for our food, can I start feeding him
text: No, not yet. Starting solid foods before around 6 months can make growth falter, according to the WHO [1]. The WHO advises starting at 6 months, beginning with small amounts and increasing gradually as the child gets older [1]. Reaching for food is a normal sign of interest at this age, but it does not mean his gut and swallowing are ready for solids. Until then, breast milk or first infant formula gives him everything he needs [2]. If he was born prematurely, ask your doctor when to start solids, as the timing may be different for him [2].

q: can I give peanut butter to my 6 month old
text: Yes, you can give peanut butter at 6 months. When you start solid foods, introduce foods that can trigger allergies one at a time so you can spot any reaction, according to the NHS [3]. Delaying peanut beyond 6 to 12 months may increase the risk of developing an allergy to it [3]. If your baby already has a diagnosed food allergy or eczema, or you have a family history of allergies, talk to your doctor first [3].

q: what foods should I start with for a baby who just turned 6 months
text:
Around 6 months, milk alone no longer covers a baby's energy and nutrient needs, so solid foods should start now [1]. Begin with small amounts and increase them gradually as your baby grows, and offer a variety of foods alongside breast milk or formula [1][2]. At first, how much they eat matters less than getting used to eating [2].

A few things to keep in mind:

- Introduce one food at a time so you can spot any allergic reaction, such as a rash, diarrhoea or vomiting [5].
- Avoid honey and cow's milk before 12 months, and unpasteurised foods and drinks [5].
- Avoid choking hazards like sweets, popcorn, whole nuts and whole grapes [5].

Ask your pediatrician if you have questions about starting solids or about foods like peanut [5].

q: how much water can a 9 month old drink
text: For a 9-month-old, breast milk or formula stays the main drink, and it is offered on demand rather than in a set amount [2]. The AEP recommends keeping at least two servings of dairy a day, around 500 ml, once the diet becomes more varied [2]. Water itself is not given a fixed quantity in these guidelines; what they do set is a limit on salt, under 1 g a day before 12 months, because a baby's kidneys are too immature to handle much [3]. During illness, offer more fluids, including more frequent breastfeeding [1]. If you are unsure how much your baby needs, ask your doctor.

q: my baby refuses vegetables but eats fruit all day
text: A varied diet with fruit and vegetables is what the AEP recommends, and it is normal for a young child to prefer one over the other at first [3]. The taste for different flavours, including bitter ones like some vegetables, is built from an early age, and early exposure to many flavours can reduce the risk of refusing new foods later [3]. Keep offering vegetables in different forms — puréed, mashed or in small pieces — and at any of the daily meals, without forcing [3]. Whole fruit is better than fruit juice, which offers no nutritional benefit over whole fruit and can displace other foods [3]. If your child is constipated, more fluids, fibre and fruit and vegetables can help, according to the SEUP [5].

q: can a 7 month old eat eggs every day
text: Yes, eggs can be part of a 7-month-old's diet every day. The AEP says protein-rich foods like eggs should be offered daily, in a varied way, especially those rich in iron [5]. Eggs are also one of the foods most often linked to allergy, but delaying them past 6 months does not prevent allergy, and early introduction in small amounts may even help [3]. Offer them cooked and mashed or in small pieces, and always supervise meals [5][4].

q: my baby is 8 months and gets constipated after starting solids
text: Constipation means fewer than three poos a week, and the poo can be hard, dry and painful to pass — it usually lasts a short time and is not serious, according to MedlinePlus [1]. For an 8-month-old on solids, the SEUP advises more fluids, preferably water, and more fibre-rich meals such as fruit, vegetables and wholegrain cereals, without replacing fruit with juice, which has little fibre [3]. Most cases in children (95%) are not caused by any illness, and it is not essential that a child poos every day [3]. See your doctor if it is not getting better with these changes, if there is blood in the poo, or if your baby has significant tummy pain, is very down and complaining, or is vomiting repeatedly and keeping nothing down [2][3].

q: how often should a newborn poop

q: my toddler has very hard poop and cries when he goes

Hard, painful poops are constipation: the stool is hard and dry and it can hurt to pass [3]. The main sign is stool that is harder and less frequent than usual, sometimes with tummy pain, bloating, or a feeling of not finishing [2]. Small tears around the anus can make it hurt more [4].

q: what can I give my 2 year old for constipation

Do not replace fruit with juice, because juice has little fibre [1]. q: when can babies have cow's milk instead of formula
text: No, cow's milk should not replace formula before 12 months. The AAP recommends all infants be fed breast milk or iron-fortified formula until at least 12 months of age, and does not recommend regular cow's milk for children under 1 year old [5]. The NHS says other milks, including cows' milk, should not be introduced as a main drink until 12 months of age [4]. Cow's milk does not contain all the nutrients your baby needs and is hard for them to digest [1]. After 1 year, whole milk is the one to give, not skim or reduced-fat milk [5].

q: how much sleep should a 2 year old get
text: Two-year-olds generally need about 11 to 14 hours of sleep in total, including a nap, according to the PUC Chile manual [2]. Around this age most children have dropped the morning nap and sleep once in the afternoon, with the rest at night, and the nap usually disappears by about age 4 [1]. Night waking is normal: between 20% and 40% of children under 3 wake at night, and they should be able to settle back to sleep on their own [2]. Keeping a consistent bedtime and sleep place helps [5]. If your child seems unwell or very tired during the day despite enough hours, see your doctor.

q: my 9 month old suddenly wakes up every two hours at night
text:
It is common at this age, and most night waking in babies is due to habits rather than illness, according to the PUC Chile manual [5]. Insomnia is one of the most frequent sleep problems in infants, and in healthy children it is usually linked to environmental changes or to feeding and sleep routines [5]. It does not affect growth, though it can leave everyone more irritable [5].

If your baby seems unwell, note that fever and lack of sleep can also trigger sudden terrified waking, according to MedlinePlus [2].

See your doctor if the waking comes with fever, poor feeding, or your baby seems unwell.

q: my toddler snores every night but seems okay during the day
text: Snoring is common in young children: about 10% of them snore, and some are simply "physiological snorers" with nothing wrong, according to the PUC Chile manual [1]. The most frequent risk factor in small children is enlarged adenoids and tonsils, along with allergies, obesity and a family history of sleep breathing problems [1]. Signs that it is more than simple snoring include loud snoring with waking, gasping as if choking, restless sleep and increased breathing effort [1]. If you notice pauses in breathing or any of those signs, have your child seen by your doctor.

text: A cough that comes mainly at night can be a sign of asthma in small children, according to the SEUP [2]. Asthma makes the airways narrow, which causes coughing, wheezing and chest tightness [6]. In preschool children, the most common trigger of this kind of cough is a viral respiratory infection [1]. Diagnosing asthma in a 4-year-old is not straightforward, because the symptoms overlap with other childhood illnesses and lung function tests are usually not possible at this age [3]. If you are worried about his breathing, see your doctor.

q: my son has asthma and is using albuterol more than usual
text: Using a reliever inhaler more often than usual is one of the signs that the asthma is not controlled, and the SEUP says you should go to a health centre if inhalations are needed very often, every two hours or less [6]. Salbutamol opens the airways and relieves symptoms, but it does not treat the inflammation behind them, which is what steroid inhalers do [2]. The SEUP notes that most flare-ups are mild and can be managed at home with bronchodilators, and symptoms usually settle within a few days, though they can last up to a week [3]. See a doctor promptly if he is very restless or drowsy, turns blue or pale, or his breathing gets faster with ribs or chest pulling in [6]. Always give the inhaler with a spacer, never straight into the mouth [6].

q: she is making a strange noise when she breathes but is still smiling
text: A strange noise while breathing can be a sign of croup, which is an inflammation of the voice box and windpipe that causes noisy, high-pitched breathing and a barking cough, according to MedlinePlus [3]. Most viral cases are mild and can be treated at home, but croup can occasionally become serious and interfere with breathing [3]. Watch for difficulty breathing — ribs pulling in, the chest sinking, fast breathing, or tiredness — and if that appears, your child needs to be seen [1][4]. If you are worried about your child's breathing, contact your doctor promptly [3].

q: what are signs that a child is having trouble breathing

Signs that a child is having trouble breathing include breathing faster than usual, the ribs pulling in or the chest sinking, and tiredness when walking or running, according to the SEUP [1]. Chest pain when breathing is another sign to watch for [1].

See a doctor straight away if the child becomes floppy, sleepy or very irritable, or if the breathing difficulty gets worse [1].

q: can a fever cause febrile seizures
banner: 🚨 Call 911 now or go to the emergency department. | Reason: Abnormal movements / seizure
text:
Yes, a fever can cause a febrile seizure, according to the NHS [2]. It can happen when a child has a high temperature, and although it looks frightening, it is unlikely to harm your child or cause long-term effects [2]. They usually affect children between 6 months and 6 years old, and most last 2 to 3 minutes [4]. Most febrile seizures do not need treatment, but your child will need to be checked in hospital after a first one [5]. You cannot prevent febrile seizures [5].

If your child is having a seizure now: check the time it starts and ends, protect their head with your hands or something soft, and remove nearby dangerous objects [6]. After it ends, put your child in the recovery position and make sure nothing is in their mouth or throat [6].

q: my child was bitten by a mosquito and the area is very swollen
text:
A swollen area after a mosquito bite is common, and most bites are harmless and get better in a few days [2][4]. q: my 3 year old was stung by a bee on the hand
text:
A bee sting on the hand usually causes only local pain, redness and swelling, according to MedlinePlus [2]. Allergies to insect stings can range from mild to severe, and a severe reaction called anaphylaxis can be life-threatening [2].

Watch for a reaction affecting more than one part of the body in the minutes after the sting, according to the SEUP: itching of the skin or scalp, swelling of the eyelids, lips or ears, widespread intense redness, hives, difficulty breathing, sneezing, dizziness, loss of consciousness or vomiting [3]. Anaphylaxis is uncommon, affecting about 1% of people [3].

If any of those signs appear, get emergency help straight away [3].

q: my 3 year old has a fever of 104 F but is drinking and playing
text:
104 °F = 40 °C.

A fever is a sign the body is fighting an infection, and it is not by itself a sign that something serious is going on, according to the SEUP [3]. Most often it lasts 2 to 4 days, and it can last longer without meaning the child is worse [4]. It is also common for a fever not to come all the way down after paracetamol or ibuprofen, and that does not mean the illness is more serious [4]. Keep offering fluids, since drinking well helps prevent dehydration [1]. Do not give aspirin to a child [1].

See a doctor if the child becomes drowsy, looks pale, or develops small red spots that do not fade when you press them [4].

q: my baby has a temperature of 100.4, is that considered a fever
text:
100.4 °F = 38 °C.

If your baby is under 3 months old, a temperature of 100.4 °F needs a doctor the same day [5].

For an older baby, yes — 100.4 °F is a fever. A normal temperature is usually around 98.6 °F (37 °C (98.6 °F)), and a fever is a temperature higher than normal, according to MedlinePlus [6]. A fever is not a disease; it is usually a sign the body is fighting an infection [6].

You can usually look after them at home, and the temperature should come down over 1 to 4 days, according to the NHS [2]. Offer plenty of fluids, keep checking on them including at night, and give paracetamol or ibuprofen only if they are distressed or uncomfortable — check the leaflet or ask a pharmacist whether it suits your child [2]. Do not give aspirin to a child under 16 [5].

See a doctor if your baby is not feeding, is not their usual self, has a rash, or the fever lasts 5 days or more [5].

q: my 10 year old says he feels dizzy after playing outside in the heat
text: Dizziness is one of the signs of heat exhaustion, along with tiredness, headache, nausea, heavy sweating and cramps in the arms, legs or stomach, according to the NHS [2]. If your son is showing these signs, he needs to be cooled down and given fluids [2]. Move him to a cool, shaded place, take off extra clothing, apply cool wet cloths to his forehead, neck and armpits, offer him cool water in small sips, and use a fan to help bring his temperature down [6]. Heat exhaustion usually does not need emergency medical help if he can cool down within 30 minutes, but if it turns into heatstroke it must be treated as an emergency [2]. To prevent it happening again, keep him well hydrated, avoid the sun during the hottest hours, and dress him in light, loose clothing [4][5].

text:
A rash that turns white when you press on it is called a blanching rash, and it is common in hives. Hives usually get better within a few days and you can often treat them yourself, according to the NHS [2]. The main symptom is an itchy rash that can be raised bumps or patches, appear anywhere on the body, and feel itchy, sting or burn [2]. In childhood, most hives are caused by an infection, and an allergic cause is less common, according to the SEUP [3]. The bumps are red and raised, and they move around: as they appear in one area they fade from another [3].

See a doctor if your child has trouble swallowing or breathing, or if the rash does not improve [4].

q: what are the side effects of the chickenpox vaccine
text:
Most side effects of the chickenpox vaccine are mild and do not last long, according to the NHS [1]. They can include swelling or pain where the injection was given, a high temperature, and a rash either at the injection site or more widespread, usually within a month of vaccination [1]. Serious side effects, such as a severe allergic reaction, are very rare, and the person who vaccinates your child is trained to treat them immediately [1].

The combined MMRV vaccine can cause a raised, blotchy rash, feeling unwell and a high temperature about 6 to 10 days afterwards, and swelling around the face or aching joints about 2 to 3 weeks afterwards [2]. A spotty rash like chickenpox may appear at the injection site about 3 to 4 weeks after vaccination; it may contain infectious chickenpox virus, so it should be covered with clothes [2].

In the United States, the ages at which these vaccines are given follow the national immunization schedule.

A lump behind the ear in a baby is often a sign of an ear infection, which is very common in children and usually gets better on its own within 3 days, according to the NHS [2]. Babies with an ear infection may rub or pull their ear, be irritable or restless, or be off their food [2]. The most frequent symptom is earache, which is often worse at night, and babies may also have a fever or feed poorly, according to the SEUP [4].

While you wait to be seen, the SEUP says to treat the pain with ibuprofen or paracetamol given regularly every 6 to 8 hours for the first 1 to 2 days, and not to put anything in the ear [3]. Do not force your baby to eat if their appetite is low, and keep the ear dry [3].

q: my toddler has a swollen eyelid after waking up
text: A swollen eyelid on waking can be one of the early signs of roseola, a common infection in toddlers that also brings a sudden high temperature and cold-like symptoms such as a sore throat, runny nose and cough [3]. Those symptoms usually last 3 to 5 days, and then a pinkish-red rash appears, starting on the chest, tummy and back before spreading to the face, neck and arms [3]. The rash is not usually itchy and normally fades within 2 days [3]. You can normally look after your child at home, and they should recover within a week [3]. See your doctor if your child seems unwell in a way that worries you, or if the swelling involves the lips or tongue or they have any trouble breathing [2].

q: my child has a headache after looking at a screen for hours
text:
A headache after hours of screen time is common, and most headaches go away on their own and are not a sign of something more serious [5]. It helps to drink plenty of water, rest, and relax, since stress can make headaches worse [5]. Avoiding long periods straining the eyes, for example by looking at a screen, can also help [2]. In most cases headaches in children last minutes or hours and improve with rest and the usual painkillers [4].

See a doctor if the headache is very intense and does not respond to the usual treatment or keeps getting worse, if it wakes your child at night, or if there is vomiting, drowsiness, or difficulty moving an arm or leg [1][6].

q: my 5 year old complains that his stomach hurts before he poops
text:
Stomach pain before pooing is a common symptom of constipation, according to the SEUP: the stools become harder and more painful to pass, and this can cause tummy pain, bloating and a feeling of not having finished [2][3]. Most cases of childhood constipation (95%) are not caused by any illness [1].

To help, offer more fluids, especially water, and more fibre — fruit, vegetables, and wholegrain cereals and bread. Don't replace fruit with juice, as juice has little fibre [1].

See a doctor if the pain is severe, if he is very down and complaining a lot, if there is blood in the stools, or if he vomits repeatedly and can't keep down solids or liquids [1].

q: my daughter has stomach pain and hasnt pooped in three days
text:
It's likely constipation: not having a poo at least 3 times in the last week, or pooing less often than usual, with poo that is dry, hard or lumpy, and straining or pain when passing it [3]. Stomach ache and feeling bloated are common too [3]. Constipation means fewer than three bowel movements a week, and in most cases it lasts a short time and is not serious [6]. It's not important that a child has a bowel movement every day — the rhythm varies from person to person [1][6].

To help: offer more liquids, preferably water, and more foods with fiber such as fruit, vegetables and wholegrain cereals, without replacing fruit with juice [1]. Don't give laxatives or enemas without checking with your doctor [1].

See your doctor if the pain is severe, if she seems very unwell and complains a lot, if there is blood in the stool, or if she vomits repeatedly and can't keep down food or drink [1].

q: my son has diarrhea but wants to eat normally
text: It is not necessary to fast: children should keep eating a practically normal diet unless a doctor says otherwise, according to the SEUP [1]. Offer food in smaller amounts and more often, respecting your son's appetite [1]. Avoid fatty foods, sweets and juices, and skip sports drinks because they have too much sugar and the wrong electrolytes for a child with diarrhea [1]. Dairy is fine, and breastfeeding can continue as usual or more often if he wants it [1]. See a doctor if he vomits a lot or cannot keep solids or liquids down, or if the vomit is green, bloody or looks like coffee grounds [1].

q: my baby vomited once after drinking a full bottle very fast
text: A single vomit after a fast feed is not one of the warning signs the SEUP lists for vomiting in children [1]. The signs that mean you should have your baby seen are vomiting two or more feeds in a baby under 3 months, vomiting a lot or not keeping down solids or liquids, green or bloody vomit or vomit that looks like coffee grounds, or being drowsy, floppy, very thirsty, sunken-eyed, crying without tears or passing little urine [1]. If your baby is under 3 months and has vomited two or more feeds, or has any of those signs, they should be checked [1]. Otherwise, keep offering fluids and feeds; the main risk with vomiting is dehydration, according to the SEUP [3].

q: my 2 year old vomited during the night and is fine this morning
text: A single night of vomiting that has settled by morning is usually not serious in a healthy child, according to MedlinePlus [2]. Vomiting is often the first sign of gastroenteritis, an inflammation of the stomach and intestines that also causes diarrhoea [6]. The main risk is dehydration, so offer your child oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts after each loose stool or vomit, as the SEUP advises [5]. Keep offering their normal food in smaller, more frequent portions, and avoid fatty foods, sweets and juices [3]. See a doctor if the vomiting becomes frequent, if they cannot keep fluids down, or if the vomit is green, bloody or looks like coffee grounds [3].

q: my child has a fever but his hands are freezing cold
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Cold hands and feet in a child with fever: it may be poor circulation, get it checked
text: If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day. For an older child, cold hands and feet with a fever are common: when the body raises its temperature, it narrows the blood vessels in the skin to keep the heat in, and that is why the hands and feet feel cold, according to the SEUP [7]. A fever is the body's normal response to infection, not an illness in itself [5]. Offer plenty of fluids and dress them normally — do not bundle them up or sponge them down to cool them [2][6]. If they are uncomfortable, the usual antipyretic your paediatrician recommends can be given; the dose depends on their age and weight [6].

q: she feels hot but the thermometer says 98.6
text:
A temperature of 98.6°F is normal, so what you are feeling may not be a fever at all. A normal temperature varies from child to child, and a high temperature is 38°C (100.4°F) or more, according to the NHS [2]. If your child has just had a bath or been wrapped in a blanket, their temperature can read higher for a short time — wait a few minutes and try again [2]. What matters most is how she seems in herself: fever is treated for the child's comfort, not for the number itself, and the usual aim is to keep her well hydrated, in a ventilated room, and not over-wrapped, according to the SEUP [1]. It is normal for her to have less appetite, so do not force her to eat, but offer plenty of fluids [1]. See a doctor if she seems unwell, has a seizure, or you notice small red spots that do not fade when you press them [2][5].

q: my baby has a temperature of 105 F, what should I do
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Fever above 40.5 °C (105 °F)
text:
105 °F = 40.6 °C.

If your baby is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day. For an older child, a high temperature is very common and usually returns to normal within 1 to 4 days, according to the NHS [3].

You can usually look after them at home: give plenty of fluids, keep breastfeeding as normal if you are, watch for signs of dehydration, and check on them regularly, including during the night [4]. If they are distressed or uncomfortable, you can give either paracetamol or ibuprofen — check the leaflet to make sure the medicine suits your child, and ask a pharmacist or doctor if you are unsure [4]. The dose depends on your child's age and weight, so follow the leaflet or your doctor's advice.

Get medical advice if you are worried about your child, or if the paracetamol or ibuprofen is not helping [4].

q: my son fell yesterday and now he is acting confused
text:
Confusion after a head injury is one of the symptoms the SEUP lists for a head trauma, along with headache, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness [1]. The SEUP also says to watch for disorientation or confusion in the 24 hours after a blow to the head, and to go to the emergency department if there is any behaviour or attitude that worries you [4][5]. MedlinePlus lists growing confusion, restlessness or agitation among the warning signs of a moderate to severe head injury, and says to seek help immediately for these [3].

Go to the emergency department now.

q: she hit her head last week and has been completely normal until today
text: Most head injuries are not serious, but it's important to get medical help for any symptoms, according to the NHS [3]. A head injury can cause concussion, a temporary brain injury that can last a few weeks [3]. Watch for warning signs: being sick, dizziness, or any other symptom that worries you [3]. Symptoms that last more than 2 weeks should be checked by your doctor [6].

q: my child says he feels like he cant catch his breath but his oxygen monitor says 99
text: A feeling of not being able to catch your breath is something to take seriously even when the oxygen reading looks normal, because difficulty breathing is a warning sign in itself. According to the SEUP, you should watch for difficulty breathing — ribs pulling in, the chest sinking, fast breathing, or getting tired when walking or running — and go to the emergency department when breathing difficulty appears [1]. The NHS also says to get medical help if your child is unwell and getting worse, or has difficulty breathing [3]. Trust what you see in your child, not only the monitor: if he is struggling to breathe, get him seen.

q: my daughter is breathing fast because she is crying, should I be worried
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Breathing difficulty: fast breathing, wheezing, ribs pulling in
text: Fast breathing while crying is expected, and it settles once she calms. What the SEUP says to watch for at home is difficulty breathing — ribs pulling in, the chest sinking, or tiring when walking or running [2]. If that appears, or she becomes floppy, sleepy or very irritable, the SEUP says to go to the emergency department [2]. The NHS describes faster breathing as a sign of a more serious infection such as bronchiolitis or pneumonia, and says to get medical help if you are worried your child is seriously ill [4]. Trust your instinct: if the fast breathing continues after she stops crying, or she looks unwell, have her seen.

q: he has a cough and is breathing normally when asleep
text:
A cough on its own, with normal breathing during sleep, is common in young children and is often the start of a cold-like illness [1][3]. In bronchiolitis, symptoms usually begin like an ordinary cold with cough and mucus, and breathing difficulty, if it appears, tends to show up after 2 to 4 days [3]. Most cases are mild and can be managed at home with follow-up by your paediatrician [5].

Watch for breathing that gets faster, ribs pulling in or the chest sinking, tiredness when walking or running, or chest pain when breathing — these mean you should seek urgent care [1]. Also seek care if he becomes floppy, sleepy or very irritable, or if breathing becomes difficult [1].

q: my baby is sleeping more today but wakes up and drinks normally
text: Some babies sleep much more than others, and every baby has their own pattern of waking and sleeping, according to the NHS [1]. All babies change their sleep patterns, and growth spurts, teething and illnesses can all affect how your baby sleeps [2]. If your baby is feeding normally when they wake, that fits with what the NHS describes as normal variation [1]. If you are worried about their sleep or want advice on routines, speak to your pediatrician [2].

q: my child has a rash after taking amoxicillin, is it an allergy
text:
A rash is the most common type of reaction to a medicine, and medicines are one of the common causes of hives, according to MedlinePlus [5][3]. Hives are raised, reddish, sometimes itchy patches that often go away on their own, though a serious case may need medicine or an injection [3].

A medicine rash can be a drug allergy, but not every rash after amoxicillin is one — only a doctor can tell [5]. Get medical help right away if there is swelling of the face, lips or tongue, trouble breathing, wheezing, vomiting, dizziness or fainting, as these can be signs of a severe allergic reaction [4][2].

q: my daughter has hives after eating eggs but no trouble breathing
text:
Hives are itchy raised red patches that move around, appearing in one area as they fade from another, according to the SEUP [1]. In childhood most hives are caused by an infection, and an allergic cause is less common [1]. They can come with swelling of the hands, feet, elbows or face, and only exceptionally with difficulty breathing or swallowing [1].

Watch for trouble breathing or swallowing, or swelling of the face — if that happens, your daughter needs to be seen straight away [1].

q: my son has swelling of his lips after eating something new
banner: 🚨 Call 911 now or go to the emergency department. | Reason: Suspected severe allergic reaction (swollen lips/eyelids with breathing difficulty, vomiting or dizziness)
text: Swelling of the lips is a common symptom of a food allergy, and it can affect different parts of the body at the same time, according to the NHS [4]. Food allergy symptoms usually start between a few minutes and two hours after eating the food, and swelling of the face, tongue or lips is one of them, according to MedlinePlus [2]. q: my child has a 102 fever but is running around like nothing happened
text:
102 °F = 38.9 °C.

A fever is the body's normal response to an infection, and it is not an illness in itself [6]. A child who is running around and playing is showing you how they feel, and how a child looks and behaves matters more than the number on the thermometer [6]. Fever rarely goes above 40.5°C (104.9 °F) on its own, and there is no evidence that it causes harm by itself [6].

You can help with physical measures first: take off extra clothing, offer fluids, reduce activity, and a lukewarm bath only if the child is comfortable [6]. If the fever is causing discomfort, paracetamol or ibuprofen can be used, with the dose based on the child's weight [5].

See a doctor if the child becomes drowsy, floppy, has trouble breathing, or is not drinking.

q: my 7 year old has vomiting and diarrhea but no fever
text:
Vomiting and diarrhea without fever are common in gastroenteritis, which usually is not serious, according to MedlinePlus [1]. Most children get better on their own with rest and plenty of fluids and electrolytes [4]. Keep offering food in smaller amounts and more often, and avoid fatty foods, sweets and juices; sports drinks should be avoided because they have too much sugar and the wrong electrolytes for a child with diarrhea, according to the SEUP [2]. Oral rehydration solution is the main treatment, and the biggest risk of vomiting is dehydration [6].

See a doctor if the diarrhea lasts more than a day, if the vomiting is frequent, if there is severe belly pain, or if there are signs of dehydration such as thirst, dry mouth, urinating less than usual, or no tears when crying [1].

q: my son is 4 and weighs 25 pounds, is that too little
text: Whether 25 pounds is too little for a 4-year-old depends on his height, not on the weight alone. For children under 5, the WHO assesses weight in relation to height: overweight is a weight-for-height above two standard deviations over the median, and obesity above three [1]. The PUC Chile manual likewise uses the weight-for-height index to define both deficit and excess from one month of age onward [4]. So the number on its own cannot tell you if he is underweight — his height has to be measured alongside it. Bring both measurements to your doctor, who can plot them on the growth curve for his age and sex [5].

q: my baby was born early and I am not sure when to start solids
text: For a baby born early, there are no clear recommendations, and the usual guidance for full-term babies cannot be applied directly, according to the AEP [4]. Premature babies are a varied group with special nutritional needs, so when to start solids should be decided individually [4]. Based on the limited evidence available, a corrected age of 6 months may be an appropriate time to begin for most premature babies [4]. It also helps to watch for signs that your baby is developmentally ready, since not all children reach these skills at the same age [4]. Ask your baby's doctor for advice on the right time for your child.

q: my 9 month old still has no teeth, is that normal
text: It is usually normal: a first tooth typically appears between 4 and 8 months of age, according to MedlinePlus [4]. Even before any teeth come through, it is important to care for your baby's mouth and gums [4]. Wipe the gums with a damp washcloth after each meal, and do not put your baby to bed with a bottle of milk, juice or sugar water — use only water for bedtime bottles [4]. Start using a soft toothbrush instead of a washcloth as soon as the first tooth shows [4]. Ask your health care provider whether your baby needs oral fluoride [4].

q: my 18 month old only says a few words
text:
At 18 months, saying only a few words is not by itself a red flag: the first year usually brings 2 to 3 words, and around 18 months children typically have 20 to 30 words, according to the PUC Chile manual [4]. See your doctor if your child says no words at all, does not walk on their own, or loses words or social skills they had before [2].

text: Losing words your child used to say is a warning sign that should be checked, according to the SEUP [6]. q: can my baby get the flu from me
text: Yes, your baby can catch the flu from you: it spreads easily between people when they cough or sneeze, according to the WHO [5]. q: my child has RSV, what can I do at home
text: There is no specific treatment for an RSV infection, and it often gets better on its own in one or two weeks, so you can usually look after your child at home, according to the NHS [2]. Keep the nose clear with nasal washes, offer small frequent feeds to keep them well fed and hydrated, and hold them in a semi-upright position to help them breathe [3]. If there is fever, an anti-fever medicine can be used, and keep them strictly away from tobacco smoke [3]. Most bronchiolitis is mild and improves within two weeks, though the cough can last longer [1]. Watch their breathing, how well they feed, their colour and general state, and their fever [1]. See a doctor if their general state worsens, they are floppy, sleepy or very irritable, or they have difficulty breathing [5].

Diarrhea after travel to a developing country is often traveler's diarrhea, caused by eating or drinking contaminated food or water, according to MedlinePlus [3]. q: my son has a rash after swimming in a lake
text:
A rash that comes up after swimming in a lake is often hives, which are raised, itchy patches that can appear anywhere on the body and look pink or red on white skin, though the colour is harder to see on brown or black skin [2]. In childhood, most hives are caused by an infection, and an allergic cause is less common [1]. The patches are evanescent: as they appear in one area they fade from another [1].

At home, watch for difficulty swallowing or breathing, avoid rubbing the skin or very hot baths and showers, and do not put powders or creams on the skin or give syrups without asking your paediatrician [3]. A child with hives can eat their usual food without introducing new foods [3]. See a doctor if your son has trouble breathing or swallowing, or if the rash does not settle [1][3].

q: my child has been bitten by mosquitoes while visiting Nigeria
text:
Mosquito bites usually just itch, and most insect bites are not serious and get better in a few days, according to MedlinePlus [1][2]. But mosquitoes in some parts of the world, including Nigeria, can spread malaria, and children under 5 are at higher risk of severe infection [3][6].

Malaria can cause fever, chills and headache, and the first symptoms can be mild and hard to recognise [6]. If your child develops a fever, chills or flu-like symptoms, they should be seen by a doctor, because malaria is preventable and curable and treatment works best early [5][6].

To protect against further bites: use mosquito repellent, sleep under a mosquito net, and wear long sleeves and trousers at dusk [4].

q: what should I know about malaria symptoms in a child returning from Africa
text: The first symptoms of malaria are usually fever, headache and chills, and they typically appear 10 to 15 days after the bite of an infected mosquito, according to the WHO [2]. Because these early symptoms look like many other febrile illnesses, it is easy to mistake them for something else, so testing as soon as possible is advised [2]. Children under 5 are at higher risk of severe infection [2]. Severe signs include extreme tiredness, confusion, seizures, difficulty breathing, dark or bloody urine, yellowing of the eyes and skin, and unusual bleeding — these need emergency care quickly [2]. Untreated falciparum malaria can become severe and cause death within 24 hours [1]. If your child becomes unwell after returning from Africa, see your doctor promptly and mention the travel.

q: my baby has been coughing and vomiting mucus
text:
Coughing and vomiting mucus is common with a stomach bug or a cold, and vomiting usually stops in 1 or 2 days, according to the NHS [3]. Keep feeding your baby as normal — breast milk or formula at its usual strength, never watered down [3][4]. Offer smaller amounts more often, and avoid fruit juice, fizzy drinks and sports drinks, which have too much sugar [3][4].

See a doctor if your baby is under 3 months and has vomited two or more feeds, is sleepy or floppy, has sunken eyes, cries without tears, is very thirsty, or is passing little urine [1]. Also seek care if the vomit is green, bloody or looks like coffee grounds, or if they cannot keep any fluids down [1][4].

q: my child coughs mostly at night but is fine during the day
text: A cough that comes mostly at night and is fine during the day can be a sign of asthma: children may have a cough, sometimes at night, along with a feeling of breathlessness, according to the SEUP [3]. q: my daughter fainted for a few seconds at school and feels fine now
text:
A brief loss of consciousness like this is called a syncope: a sudden, short loss of consciousness that happens when not enough blood or oxygen reaches the brain, according to the SEUP [2]. It is often triggered by heat, pain, fear, nervousness, standing still for a long time, or getting up suddenly [2]. Children usually recover quickly after a period of rest, within a couple of minutes [5]. If it happens again, having them sit or lie down as soon as they feel unwell can prevent the faint and the fall [5].

See a doctor if the faint lasted more than 3 to 5 minutes, happened during exercise or while sitting, or came with palpitations, chest pain, jerking of the limbs or passing urine [6].

q: my child fell from a second story window but seems okay
text:

- Trouble speaking or walking, weakness in the arms or legs, dilated pupils [3][5]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [5]

q: my child has been sick twice and now wants water
text: Yes, offer water — small sips often, since that is the most important thing to avoid dehydration, according to the NHS [2]. Watch for signs of dehydration: dry mouth, no tears when crying, or no wet nappies for 3 hours or more [4]. See a doctor if your child is unusually sleepy or irritable, has frequent vomiting or loose stools, or any fever in a baby [1].

q: can my baby have paracetamol after his jabs

Ask for an urgent appointment with your doctor if your baby is under 3 months old and has a temperature of 38C or higher, or is 3 to 6 months old and has a temperature of 39C or higher [6].

q: my child keeps scratching red patches on his arms
text:
Itchy, dry, red patches on the skin are typical of eczema, which is also called dermatitis, according to MedlinePlus [1]. Scratching can make the skin redder and the itch worse [1]. Eczema is not contagious, and its exact cause is not known — it is likely a mix of genetic and environmental factors [1]. It often comes and goes over a long time, and is most common in babies and children [1]. Avoiding things that irritate the skin, such as certain soaps, fabrics and lotions, can help prevent some types [1].

See your doctor if the patches do not get better, spread, or look infected.

q: my son has been constipated since we started weaning
text:
Constipation is common and in most cases it lasts a short time and is not serious, according to MedlinePlus [2]. It means fewer than three bowel movements a week, and the stool can be hard, dry and painful to pass [2]. It is not important that he has a bowel movement every day, but if his bowel habits have changed, check with your doctor [2].

What usually helps is more fluids, preferably water, and more foods with fibre — fruit, vegetables, and wholegrain cereals and bread — and not replacing fruit with juices, which have little fibre, according to the SEUP [3]. Most cases of constipation in children are not caused by any illness [3]. Do not give him laxatives or enemas without asking your doctor [3].

See your doctor if it is not getting better with these changes, if he is regularly constipated or bloated, if there is blood in his poo, or if he has tummy pain [1].

q: when can I start weaning my baby
text:
Start around 6 months old, according to the NHS [6]. At first, how much your baby eats matters less than getting them used to eating, and they will still get most of their energy and nutrients from breast milk or first infant formula [6]. If your baby was born prematurely, ask your health visitor or doctor for advice on when to start [6].

You can offer finger foods and let your baby feed themselves, or spoon-feed purées, or a mix of both — there is no right or wrong way [3]. What matters most is that your baby eats a wide variety of food and gets the nutrients they need [3].

q: my child has loose motions since morning what should I give
text:
Give an oral rehydration solution to replace the fluids and electrolytes lost, according to the WHO [1]. It is a mix of clean water, salt and sugar, and it is the most important step to avoid dehydration [1]. Keep offering nutritious food and milk during the episode, not only fluids [1]. See a doctor if the child is very thirsty, cries without tears, wees little or has sunken eyes, is very irritable or drowsy, refuses to drink, or has blood in the stools [3].

q: my 4 year old is vomiting and not eating
text:
Keep offering fluids as oral rehydration solution, and let your child keep eating a fairly normal diet — no need to fast, according to the SEUP [2][4]. Offer smaller amounts more often, and respect their appetite [4]. Avoid fatty foods, sweets and juices, and skip sports drinks, which have too much sugar for a child [4]. The main risk from vomiting is dehydration [2].

See a doctor if your child vomits a lot and cannot keep down solids or liquids, vomits even without taking anything, or the vomit is green, bloody or looks like coffee grounds [1][4]. Also seek care if they are drowsy, limp, very thirsty, have sunken eyes, cry without tears or pass little urine [1].

q: my son has a cough and cold for 5 days

A cold usually starts with a blocked or runny nose, sneezing, a sore throat and a cough, and symptoms often last 10 to 14 days, according to MedlinePlus [5]. q: can I give ORS after every loose stool
text: Yes — oral rehydration salts are one of the key measures for treating diarrhoea, according to the WHO [6]. They are a mixture of clean water, salt and sugar that is absorbed in the small intestine and replaces the water and electrolytes lost in the stools [6]. Zinc supplements are also part of the treatment: they shorten a diarrhoea episode by about 25% and reduce stool volume by around 30% [6]. Keep giving nutrient-rich foods, including breast milk, during the episode [6]. See a health professional if the diarrhoea persists, if there is blood in the stool, or if there are signs of dehydration [6].

q: my child has not passed urine much today
text:
A child who is passing much less urine than usual may be dehydrated, according to MedlinePlus [1]. In infants and young children, other signs include a dry mouth and tongue, crying without tears, and no wet diapers for 3 hours or more [1]. q: my 6 month old has started solids, can I give banana
text: Yes, you can give banana now. Babies start solid foods around 6 months, and fruits are part of the foods offered from 6 to 12 months, according to the AEP [3][4]. q: my baby has diarrhea after we came back from a trip
text:
Diarrhoea is treated by replacing lost fluids and electrolytes to prevent dehydration, according to MedlinePlus [2]. For children, that means oral rehydration solutions [2]. The WHO also lists zinc supplements as a key treatment: they reduce how long the diarrhoea lasts and how much stool is passed [6]. Keep giving nutrient-rich foods, including breast milk, during the episode [6].

See a health professional if the diarrhoea is persistent, if there is blood in the stool, or if there are signs of dehydration [6]. Signs of dehydration include much thirst, crying without tears, little urine, or sunken eyes [1].

q: my 5 year old has stomach pain and constipation
text:
Stomach ache is a common symptom in children and is usually harmless and short-lived, often caused by constipation, gas or a tummy bug, according to the SEUP [2]. Constipation is likely if your child has not pooed at least 3 times in the last week, or the poo is large, dry, hard or lumpy, or they strain or feel they have not fully emptied [1]. A stomach ache and feeling bloated or sick can go with it [1].

To help, offer more fluids, especially water, and more fibre — wholegrain cereals and bread, fruit and vegetables — and don't replace fruit with juice, which has little fibre [3]. Most cases improve with these diet changes, though a paediatrician may sometimes add a laxative [3]. Don't give laxatives or enemas without asking your doctor [3].

See a doctor if the pain is severe, your child is very unwell and complaining a lot, there is blood in the poo, or they vomit repeatedly and can't keep down food or drink [3].

q: my child has been in the sun and now feels dizzy
text:
Dizziness after being in the sun can be a sign of dehydration, according to the NHS [3]. Other signs to look for are thirst, headache, dark yellow pee, peeing less often than usual, tiredness, and a dry mouth, lips and tongue [3]. In babies, dehydration may also show as a sunken soft spot on the head, sunken eyes, few or no tears when crying, or fewer wet nappies than usual [3].

Get medical help straight away if there is confusion, fainting, no peeing, fast heartbeat or fast breathing, according to MedlinePlus [1].

q: my baby is not drinking milk because his nose is blocked
text:
A blocked nose from a cold is common and usually gets better within a few days, according to the NHS [3]. While their nose is blocked, babies may feed less than usual [3]. text:
A night-time cough in a 3-year-old can have several causes, and the treatment depends on which one it is. Asthma symptoms include coughing that is worse at night or early in the morning, according to MedlinePlus [3]. q: my child swallowed a little toothpaste, is it dangerous
text:
Toothpaste swallowed in small amounts is not usually dangerous, according to the SEUP [2]. If there is something solid still in the mouth and you can see it, take it out — never blindly [2]. Do not make the child vomit, and do not give water, milk or food [2]. Try to work out how much was swallowed [2].

See a doctor or call your local emergency number if the child does not respond normally, is breathing poorly, or has a bad colour [2].

q: my daughter has a fever and small red spots all over her body
text:
If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day.

A fever is a temperature of 38C or more, and it usually returns to normal within 1 to 4 days, according to the NHS [1]. A spotty rash that starts on the head or neck and spreads to the rest of the body could be measles, and the NHS says to speak to a doctor if you think your child has measles [4]. q: my son has been vomiting since morning and cannot keep ORS down
text:
If your child keeps being sick and cannot keep fluid down, that is a sign to get medical advice now, according to the NHS [1]. The main risk of vomiting is dehydration, and oral rehydration solution is the best way to replace lost fluids — give it in small, frequent sips rather than a full glass at once [4][6].

Watch for signs of dehydration: fewer wet nappies, dark or smelly pee, peeing less than usual, sunken eyes, crying without tears, drowsiness or floppiness [1][3]. Vomiting that is green, contains blood, or looks like coffee grounds also needs urgent attention [3][5].

Keep offering small amounts of fluid often, and continue breastfeeding or formula as normal [6].

q: my baby is 8 months and has fever since yesterday, can I give paracetamol syrup
text: Yes, you can give paracetamol syrup if your baby is distressed or uncomfortable — check the packaging or leaflet to make sure the medicine is suitable for an 8-month-old, according to the NHS [1]. Keep breastfeeding as normal and offer plenty of fluids, and check on them regularly, including during the night [1]. The aim of treating fever is the child's comfort, not bringing the temperature down for its own sake, and the dose is the one your paediatrician recommends, according to the SEUP [3]. Get medical advice if you are worried about your child, or if the paracetamol is not helping [1].

q: what can I give my 2 year old for diarrhoea
text: For diarrhoea, the main treatment is oral rehydration salts (ORS) — a mixture of clean water, salt and sugar — which replaces the water and electrolytes lost in the stools, according to the WHO [5]. Zinc supplements are also a key treatment: they shorten the episode by about 25% and reduce stool volume by around 30% [5]. Keep giving nutrient-rich foods, including breast milk, during the episode [5]. Do not use homemade solutions or commercial soft drinks to replace the losses, and do not give medicines for diarrhoea or vomiting without asking your paediatrician, according to the SEUP [3]. See a doctor for persistent diarrhoea, blood in the stool, or signs of dehydration such as much thirst, crying without tears, little urine, sunken eyes, marked irritability or drowsiness [3][5].

q: my 2 year old has fever and diarrhoea, what should I do
text:
For a 2-year-old with fever and diarrhoea, the main treatment is to keep giving fluids and food. The WHO lists oral rehydration salts (ORS) — a mixture of clean water, salt and sugar — as a key treatment for diarrhoea [1]. See a doctor if there is blood in the stool, signs of dehydration, or the diarrhoea persists [1]. q: my 6 month old has started eating food, what should I give first
text:
Around 6 months is the right time to start solid foods, according to the NHS [2]. At first, how much your baby eats matters less than getting them used to the idea of eating — they still get most of their energy and nutrients from breast milk or first infant formula [2].

Start with one food at a time, following your family's usual foods, to widen the diet and improve nutrition, says the AEP [4]. Include iron-rich foods as early as possible [6]. Giving a variety of foods from around 6 months helps set up healthier eating for life [2].

If your baby was born prematurely, ask your doctor for advice on when to start [2].

text:
A scald from hot water should be treated straight away: hold the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, as soon as possible and within 3 hours of it happening, according to the NHS [2]. q: my child is not drinking water and has very little urine
text: A child who is not drinking and is passing very little urine has signs of dehydration, according to MedlinePlus [4]. In babies and young children these include a dry mouth and tongue, crying without tears, not wetting nappies for 3 hours or more, unusual sleepiness or irritability, and eyes that look sunken [4]. Dehydration happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in, and not drinking enough water is one cause [3]. Get medical help immediately if there is confusion, fainting, no urine at all, fast heartbeat or fast breathing [4]. The SEUP advises offering oral rehydration solution in small amounts, and says the risk of dehydration is greater the younger the child is [6].

q: can I give ORS to my 1 year old after diarrhea
text: Yes, you can give your 1-year-old oral rehydration salts after diarrhoea. q: my 5 year old has stomach pain and constipation
text:
Stomach ache is a common symptom in children and most causes are mild and get better on their own, including constipation and gas, according to the SEUP [2]. Constipation often causes a stomach ache and bloating, and it is likely if your child has not pooed at least 3 times in the last week, or the poo is large, dry, hard or lumpy, or they strain or feel pain when they poo [1].

For a 5-year-old, the main things that help are more fluids, especially water, and more fibre from cereals, bread, fruit and vegetables — fruit rather than juice, which has little fibre [3]. Most cases of childhood constipation are not caused by any illness, and children do not need to poo every day [3]. Do not give laxatives or enemas without asking your doctor [3].

See a doctor if the pain is severe, your child is very unwell and complaining a lot, there is blood in the poo, or they vomit repeatedly and cannot keep down food or drink [3].

q: when should I start solids for my baby

If your baby was born prematurely, ask your doctor for advice on when to start [2].

A child who vomits but then wants to eat can usually keep eating: there is no need to fast, and they should carry on with a practically normal diet unless a doctor says otherwise, according to the SEUP [4]. Offer food in smaller amounts and more often, to lower the risk of vomiting again, and follow their appetite [4]. q: como se si se esta deshidratando con la diarrea
text:
Para saber si se está deshidratando, fíjate en si tiene mucha sed, llora sin lágrimas, orina poco o tiene los ojos hundidos, según la SEUP [1]. También son señales de alarma la irritabilidad marcada, la somnolencia o que responda menos de lo habitual [1]. En bebés y niños, hay que vigilar además la boca seca, orinar menos de lo habitual o no mojar los pañales durante 3 horas o más, según MedlinePlus [2].

Lo más importante es evitar la deshidratación ofreciendo solución de rehidratación oral en dosis pequeñas y tomas frecuentes, después de cada deposición líquida o vómito [3]. No uses soluciones caseras ni refrescos, y no le des medicamentos para la diarrea o los vómitos sin consultar con su pediatra [1].

Consulta cuanto antes si el niño no es capaz de beber al mismo ritmo que pierde, rechaza comer o beber, o tiene dolor abdominal intenso o deposiciones con mucha sangre [1].

q: mi hijo tiene tos seca sobre todo por la noche
text: La tos seca que empeora por la noche es un síntoma habitual del catarro de vías altas, según la SEUP: la mucosidad puede durar hasta una semana y la tos puede durar más de una semana [4][6]. En niños pequeños conviene ofrecer abundantes líquidos y hacer lavados nasales antes de dormir, preferiblemente con suero salino [4]. Mantén al niño alejado del humo y no uses jarabes para la tos ni anticatarrales, sobre todo si es menor de 6 años [4]. La tos persistente sobre todo por la noche también aparece en el asma, según la OMS, y quien tiene síntomas de asma debe consultar a un profesional de la salud [5]. Consulta a tu doctor si la tos dura semanas, si le cuesta respirar o si lo ves decaído o con mal color [2][5].

q: mi bebe tiene muchos mocos y le cuesta dormir
text:
Los mocos y la tos son los síntomas típicos del catarro de vías altas, una infección vírica muy frecuente en los primeros años, según la SEUP [3]. La mucosidad puede durar hasta una semana, y la tos incluso más [4].

Para ayudar a dormir, la SEUP recomienda hacer lavados nasales antes de dormir, preferiblemente con suero salino y nunca con agua del grifo [4]. Conviene ofrecerle líquidos abundantes y mantenerlo lejos del humo [4]. No uses mucolíticos, descongestivos ni jarabes para la tos, sobre todo si es menor de 6 años [4].

Consulta a tu pediatra si le cuesta respirar, respira más deprisa, está irritable o le cuesta comer [5].

q: le ha salido un sarpullido rojo por las piernas y le pica
text:
La urticaria son ronchas o placas rojas y elevadas que pican mucho, y en la infancia la mayoría están causadas por una infección, según la SEUP [3]. Esas lesiones aparecen en una zona y desaparecen de otras, y pueden acompañarse de hinchazón de manos, pies, codos o cara [3]. Otra causa frecuente de sarpullido rojo con picor en las piernas son las picaduras de insectos, que dan lesiones muy pruriginosas en las zonas descubiertas de la piel, según Ecimed [6]. El eccema también cursa con sequedad, comezón y sarpullido, y no es contagioso, según MedlinePlus [1].

Consulta a tu doctor si el sarpullido se extiende, se infecta con el rascado o le cuesta respirar o tragar [3][6].

q: mi hijo tiene manchas despues de tener fiebre, puede ser por la fiebre?
text:
Si el niño tiene menos de 3 meses, la fiebre necesita que lo vea un médico ese mismo día.

En un niño mayor, las manchas rojas en la piel que no desaparecen al presionarlas son un signo de alarma: hay que consultar en urgencias, según la SEUP [2]. Lo mismo ocurre si aparecen de forma súbita manchas en la piel o hinchazón de labios o párpados, sobre todo con dificultad para respirar, vómitos o mareo [6].

También conviene vigilar su estado general y que tenga buen color, y consultar si está decaído, poco reactivo o muy irritable, o si le cuesta respirar [1][2].

Si las manchas desaparecen al presionar y el niño está bien, la fiebre puede durar entre 2 y 4 días, y eso por sí solo no indica gravedad [1].

¿Qué edad tiene? Con la edad afino la respuesta.

q: se ha caido de la cama y ha vomitado una vez
banner: 🚨 Con estos síntomas hay que acudir a urgencias hoy, sin esperar. | Motivo: Vómitos tras un golpe en la cabeza
text:
Tras un golpe en la cabeza, hay que consultar en urgencias si el niño tiene menos de tres meses o si la caída fue desde más de un metro de altura, según la SEUP [1]. También si presenta un comportamiento o una actitud que preocupen [1]. El personal médico hará las exploraciones necesarias y valorará si hacen falta pruebas adicionales, aunque en la mayoría de los casos no son necesarias [1].

Mientras tanto, ofrécele líquidos en cantidades pequeñas y con frecuencia, sin forzarle a comer [3][4].

q: mi hija se ha dado un golpe en la cabeza pero esta como siempre
text:
La mayoría de los traumatismos craneales son leves y no representan un peligro, según la SEUP [6]. Aun así, conviene vigilar a la niña durante las primeras 24 horas por si aparecen señales de gravedad [6]. Los síntomas habituales de un golpe en la cabeza son dolor de cabeza, confusión, mareo, náuseas, vómitos y somnolencia [2]. En casa, puede seguir con su alimentación habitual y, si tiene dolor de cabeza, se le puede dar ibuprofeno o paracetamol en la dosis indicada por su médico [4]. Se recomienda reposo físico y mental entre 24 y 48 horas, sin deporte ni pantallas, y volver poco a poco a sus actividades [3].

Consulta a tu médico si tiene dolor de cabeza intenso o que no mejora, vómitos repetidos, desorientación o confusión, cambios en su comportamiento, dificultad para hablar o caminar, o si sale sangre o líquido claro por la nariz o los oídos [3].

q: cuando puedo empezar con los solidos con mi bebe
text:
Alrededor de los 6 meses, según la OMS: a esa edad la leche materna ya no cubre por sí sola las necesidades de energía y nutrientes del bebé, y hacen falta alimentos complementarios [3]. Empezar antes de esa edad o retrasarlo puede afectar al crecimiento [3].

No hay alimentos mejores que otros para empezar, aunque la AEP recomienda priorizar los ricos en hierro y zinc, introducirlos de uno en uno con unos días de intervalo y no añadir sal, azúcar ni edulcorantes [2].

Además de la edad, el bebé debe estar preparado: mostrar interés por la comida, haber perdido el reflejo de expulsión, poder coger comida con la mano y llevarla a la boca, y mantenerse sentado con apoyo [6].

q: mi bebe de 7 meses solo quiere fruta, pasa algo?
text: No, no pasa nada porque un bebé de 7 meses prefiera la fruta: a esta edad la fruta es un alimento adecuado dentro de la alimentación complementaria, según MedlinePlus [5]. Lo importante es que la fruta no sustituya a la leche materna o de fórmula, que sigue siendo su alimento principal, y que las frutas se laven y se pelen antes de dárselas [5]. Ofrécele también otros alimentos variados además de la fruta, para que la dieta sea completa. Si notas que el bebé deja de ganar peso, rechaza la leche o tiene diarrea, consulta con tu pediatra.

q: puede tomar leche de vaca un bebe de 10 meses
text: No, a los 10 meses no debe tomar leche de vaca: hay que evitarla antes de que cumpla un año, porque no contiene todos los nutrientes que necesita y los bebés no pueden digerirla, según MedlinePlus [1]. La leche materna es lo mejor para él y tiene todas las vitaminas y minerales que necesita [1]. Si no puede o no quiere darle pecho, existen fórmulas para lactantes [1]. Consulte con su pediatra antes de cualquier cambio en la alimentación [3].

q: mi hijo lleva varios dias sin hacer caca y le duele al hacerla
text: El estreñimiento es el aumento de la dureza de las heces, con molestias o defecación incompleta, y puede acompañarse de menos deposiciones, según la SEUP [3]. El dolor al hacer caca es habitual, sobre todo si hay fisuras anales [1]. En casa, lo principal es ofrecer más líquidos, sobre todo agua, y más comidas con fibra: frutas, verduras, cereales y pan integrales [2]. No sustituyas la fruta por zumos, porque tienen poca fibra [2]. En niños mayores ayuda sentarse en el retrete todos los días a la misma hora, mejor después de alguna comida, unos 5-10 minutos y con los pies apoyados [6]. No des laxantes ni enemas sin consultar con su pediatra [2]. Consulta si tiene dolor abdominal importante, sangre en las heces o vómitos repetidos que no le dejan ni beber [2].

q: mi bebe hace caca muy dura desde que empezamos con los solidos
text: La introducción de sólidos puede cambiar la consistencia de las heces, y la AEP recomienda aumentar progresivamente la consistencia de los alimentos, empezando por texturas grumosas y semisólidas, nunca más tarde de los 8-9 meses [6]. Ofrece agua con las comidas y alimentos ricos en fibra como frutas, hortalizas y legumbres, que forman parte del calendario orientativo de la alimentación complementaria [1]. Evita forzar o presionar con la comida: eso interfiere con la autorregulación del hambre y la saciedad [6]. Consulta con tu pediatra si las heces siguen siendo muy duras, si le cuesta mucho hacer caca o si ves sangre en el pañal.

q: mi hija tiene otitis y le duele mucho por la noche
text:
El dolor de oído es el síntoma más frecuente de la otitis media aguda, y suele ser más intenso por la noche, según la SEUP [1]. Lo fundamental es tratar el dolor: ibuprofeno o paracetamol cada 6-8 horas de forma reglada los primeros 1-2 días [4]. No eche nada en el oído para calmar el dolor y evite mojarlo, sobre todo si ha supurado [4]. Habitualmente los síntomas se resuelven en 48-72 horas con tratamiento analgésico, sin necesitar antibiótico [6].

Consulte con su pediatra si es menor de 6 meses, tiene mal estado general, fiebre de 39ºC o más, supuración por el oído, o no mejora pasadas esas 48-72 horas [6].

q: mi hijo tiene conjuntivitis y se le pegan los ojos al despertarse
text:
No hay ningún problema en limpiar los ojos con agua tibia y una gasa, según la SEUP [1]. La conjuntivitis suele mejorar en unos días, y los ojos pegados al despertar se limpian mejor con una gasa húmeda, de dentro hacia fuera, usando una distinta para cada ojo [1].

Consulta con tu pediatra si el niño está decaído, muy irritable o somnoliento, o si tiene dificultad para respirar [1].

q: mi hija tiene 40 de fiebre pero esta jugando como si nada
text:
Con 40 de fiebre, lo importante es cómo se encuentra la niña, y que esté jugando es buena señal: la fiebre es un mecanismo de defensa y no es sinónimo de gravedad, según la SEUP [4]. Lo más habitual es que dure entre 2 y 4 días, y puede durar más sin que eso indique mayor gravedad [2]. El objetivo en casa es el confort: ofrécele líquidos abundantes, no la sobreabrigues y no la bañes en agua fría [3]. Si hay malestar, el paracetamol o el ibuprofeno a la dosis que indique su pediatra pueden ayudar, pero no curan la infección [3].

Consulta a tu médico si la niña pierde el buen color o el buen estado general, o si le aparecen puntos rojos en la piel que no desaparecen al apretarlos [2].

¿Qué edad tiene? Con la edad afino la respuesta.

q: mi bebe tiene menos pañales mojados hoy
text: No mojar los pañales durante 3 horas o más es una señal de deshidratación en bebés y niños pequeños, según MedlinePlus [2]. Otros signos son la boca y la lengua secas, llorar sin lágrimas, tener mucho sueño o estar irritable, y los ojos hundidos [2]. La deshidratación puede ser leve o grave, así que conviene que un profesional de la salud valore a tu bebé [2]. Si además está confundido, se desmaya, respira rápido o tiene los latidos rápidos, busca ayuda médica de inmediato [2].
sources: [2] MedlinePlus — "Deshidratación", section "¿Cuáles son los síntomas de la deshidratación

q: no quiere beber nada desde esta mañana y tiene los labios secos
banner: 🚨 Con estos síntomas hay que acudir a urgencias hoy, sin esperar. | Motivo: Signos de deshidratación: ojos hundidos, orina poco, boca seca, vómitos persistentes o diarrea abundante >24 h
text: No ofrecerle líquidos a la fuerza no es lo indicado: hay que seguir dándole de beber, en cantidades pequeñas y más frecuentes, respetando su apetito, según la SEUP [1]. Los labios secos son una señal de deshidratación, así que lo importante ahora es ofrecerle suero de rehidratación oral poco a poco y con frecuencia [1]. Si vomita mucho o no tolera ni líquidos ni sólidos, hay que consultar de nuevo en urgencias [1]. Evita las bebidas deportivas y los zumos, porque llevan demasiado azúcar y electrolitos inadecuados [1].

q: mi hijo respira mas rapido de lo normal cuando tiene fiebre
banner: 🚨 Con estos síntomas hay que acudir a urgencias hoy, sin esperar. | Motivo: Dificultad para respirar: respira rápido, «pitido» al respirar, se marcan las costillas
text: Si el bebé tiene menos de 3 meses, la fiebre necesita que lo vea un médico ese mismo día. En un niño mayor, la fiebre es un mecanismo de defensa y no es sinónimo de gravedad [7]. Que respire más rápido de lo normal es uno de los motivos por los que la SEUP recomienda consultar en urgencias [2]. Mientras tanto, asegúrate de que esté bien hidratado, en una habitación ventilada y sin sobreabrigarlo [4]. Los antitérmicos (paracetamol o ibuprofeno) bajan la temperatura y mejoran el estado general, a la dosis que indique su pediatra [4].

q: se le marcan las costillas al respirar pero luego se pone a jugar
banner: 🚨 Llama ahora al 112 o acude a urgencias. | Motivo: Dificultad para respirar grave (se marcan las costillas, respira muy rápido, pausas en la respiración, color azulado); Dificultad para respirar: respira rápido, «pitido» al respirar, se marcan las costillas
text: Las costillas marcándose al respirar son un signo de dificultad respiratoria que hay que vigilar en casa, según la SEUP [2]. Ese esfuerzo puede aparecer en cuadros como la bronquiolitis, donde se marcan las costillas o se hunde el pecho [3], o en una crisis asmática, donde también se marcan las costillas y las clavículas al respirar [6]. Que después se ponga a jugar no quita que ese signo esté ahí: la SEUP recomienda consultar cuando aparece dificultad para respirar [2]. Mientras llega la ayuda, mantén al niño tranquilo y vigilado, y no le des jarabes ni supositorios para la tos sin consultar con su pediatra [7].

q: mi hija tiene asma y esta usando el salbutamol mas veces de lo habitual
text:
Si necesita salbutamol cada dos horas o menos, hay que acudir a un centro sanitario, según la SEUP [3]. También si la dificultad para respirar empeora —respira cada vez más deprisa, se le marcan las costillas o se le hunde el pecho—, o si está muy agitada, somnolienta, pálida o morada [3].

En casa, la SEUP indica administrar de 2 a 4 pulsaciones con cámara espaciadora, de una en una, y repetir a los 10-15 minutos; si la crisis no cede, hay que acudir lo antes posible sin olvidar la cámara [4]. El salbutamol abre las vías respiratorias y alivia los síntomas, según la OMS [6]. Si usa el inhalador de mantenimiento, debe seguir con él durante la crisis [4].
